title: Job 37:1–13
context: Elihu continues his description of the storm. He says his heart trembles at the thunder of God's voice and the lightning that reaches the ends of the earth. He speaks of snow, rain, ice, and cold as all coming at God's command, so that people and animals stop and take shelter. He concludes that God sends the clouds for correction, for his land, or for loving kindness. The storm language prepares for the LORD's speech out of the whirlwind, but Elihu is still the speaker.

verses.text: “Yes, at this my heart trembles, and is moved out of its place.
verses.arminianNotes: "Yes, at this my heart trembles." Arminian readers see Elihu responding personally to the storm with awe, his heart "moved out of its place."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Elihu models a fitting response to God's power: trembling reverence. Both traditions treat awe before God's majesty as shared ground.

verses.text: Hear, oh, hear the noise of his voice, the sound that goes out of his mouth.
verses.arminianNotes: "Hear, oh, hear the noise of his voice." Arminian readers see Elihu urging his hearers to listen to thunder as God's voice, a sign of his power and presence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers often compare Psalm 29:3, "The God of glory thunders." Thunder as God's voice is familiar biblical imagery. Elihu uses it to call Job to attention.

verses.text: He sends it out under the whole sky, and his lightning to the ends of the earth.
verses.arminianNotes: "He sends it out under the whole sky." Arminian readers see God's voice and lightning reaching "to the ends of the earth." No place is beyond his reach.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the universal scope of God's rule. The storm is not local or random but goes out under the whole sky at his direction.

verses.text: After it a voice roars. He thunders with the voice of his majesty. He doesn’t hold back anything when his voice is heard.
verses.arminianNotes: "After it a voice roars." Arminian readers see Elihu describing the thunder that follows lightning as God's majestic voice, which he "doesn’t hold back."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God "thunders with the voice of his majesty." Elihu presents the storm as a display of divine glory, a theme the LORD's speeches will deepen.

verses.text: God thunders marvelously with his voice. He does great things, which we can’t comprehend.
verses.arminianNotes: "God thunders marvelously with his voice." Arminian readers see Elihu confessing that God "does great things, which we can’t comprehend." This humility is a fitting stance before God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job and Eliphaz said similar things (9:10; 5:9). The greatness of God's works is common ground among the speakers. The dispute was never about whether God is great.

verses.text: For he says to the snow, ‘Fall on the earth,’ likewise to the shower of rain, and to the showers of his mighty rain.
verses.arminianNotes: "For he says to the snow, ‘Fall on the earth,’" Elihu declares. Arminian readers see God commanding snow and rain by his word, as a king commands his servants.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers compare Psalm 147:16, "He gives snow like wool." The LORD will later ask Job about "the storehouses of the snow" (38:22). Weather obeys God's word.

verses.text: He seals up the hand of every man, that all men whom he has made may know it.
verses.arminianNotes: "He seals up the hand of every man." Arminian readers see heavy weather stopping human work, so that people pause and recognize God's power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the purpose clause: "that all men whom he has made may know it." God's control of weather is meant to make people aware of their Maker.

verses.text: Then the animals take cover, and remain in their dens.
verses.arminianNotes: "Then the animals take cover, and remain in their dens." Arminian readers see even the animals responding to the storm, taking shelter as people do.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that all creatures are affected by God's weather. Elihu's picture includes animals, preparing for the LORD's own focus on wild creatures in chapters 38–39.

verses.text: Out of its room comes the storm, and cold out of the north.
verses.arminianNotes: "Out of its room comes the storm, and cold out of the north." Arminian readers see Elihu describing storms and cold as if they come from storerooms, ready at God's command.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the image of weather kept in chambers. The LORD will use similar language about storehouses when he speaks in 38:22.

verses.text: By the breath of God, ice is given, and the width of the waters is frozen.
verses.arminianNotes: "By the breath of God, ice is given." Arminian readers see God's breath freezing the waters, a vivid picture of his power over the natural world.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that even ice comes from God's breath. Both traditions treat God's governance of creation as shared ground, apart from Elihu's conclusions about Job.

verses.text: Yes, he loads the thick cloud with moisture. He spreads abroad the cloud of his lightning.
verses.arminianNotes: "Yes, he loads the thick cloud with moisture." Arminian readers see God filling the clouds with rain and spreading "the cloud of his lightning" across the sky.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God both loads and spreads the clouds. Elihu emphasizes God's active involvement in every part of the storm.

verses.text: It is turned around by his guidance, that they may do whatever he commands them on the surface of the habitable world,
verses.arminianNotes: "It is turned around by his guidance." Arminian readers see the clouds moving at God's direction, doing "whatever he commands them" across the habitable world.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note how clearly Elihu says that weather follows God's guidance. Nothing in the storm is left to chance. Both traditions treat this as shared ground.

verses.text: whether it is for correction, or for his land, or for loving kindness, that he causes it to come.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says God sends the clouds "whether it is for correction, or for his land, or for loving kindness." Arminian readers see God's purposes in weather as varied: discipline, care for the land, and steadfast love.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the same storm may serve different ends at God's will. Elihu does not claim to know which purpose applies in each case, which fits the book's caution about reading events.
